description: Xilinx Design Constraints are Tcl: SDC timing commands, Vivado physical and attribute constraints applied with set_property, and the report_* family that reads the results back out. Constraints are evaluated in file order against the elaborated or synthesized netlist, and every command operates on design objects returned by the get_* query commands.

tools.name: create_clock
tools.description: Define a primary clock on a port, pin or net, giving the timing engine a period, a name and a waveform. Every path in the design is timed relative to some clock, so an unconstrained clock means unconstrained paths and a misleadingly clean timing report. Use it for clocks that enter the device from outside; clocks generated inside the device by an MMCM, PLL or clock divider should be described with create_generated_clock instead.

parameters.name: -period
parameters.description: Clock period in nanoseconds (the XDC time unit). 10.000 is 100 MHz.

parameters.name: -name
parameters.description: Name of the clock object. If omitted, the clock takes the name of the source object.

parameters.name: -waveform
parameters.description: Rising and falling edge times within one period, e.g. {0 5} for 50% duty. Use it to describe shifted or non-50% clocks.

parameters.name: -add
parameters.description: Add a second clock to a source that already has one instead of replacing it; requires -name.

parameters.name: <source_objects>
parameters.description: Result of get_ports, get_pins or get_nets. A virtual clock is created by omitting the source entirely.

tools.example:
# 100 MHz differential system clock on a package pin
create_clock -period 10.000 -name sys_clk -waveform {0.000 5.000} [get_ports sys_clk_p]

# Virtual clock used only as the reference for board-level I/O delays
create_clock -period 8.000 -name virt_src_clk

report_clocks
tools.notes: MMCM/PLL outputs are auto-derived by Vivado and must not be constrained with create_clock; doing so overrides the derived clock and usually produces wrong results. Use report_clocks to see every clock, including auto-derived ones, and check_timing to find clocks you forgot to define.

tools.name: create_generated_clock
tools.description: Describe a clock that is produced inside the device from another clock, by giving its relationship to the master clock as a division, multiplication, edge list or phase shift. Vivado derives MMCM, PLL and BUFGCE_DIV outputs automatically, so this is mainly needed for clocks built out of user logic, such as a register-based divide-by-2 or a gated clock on a BUFGCE.

parameters.name: -source
parameters.description: Pin or port where the master clock enters the generating logic. Give the pin, not the clock name.

parameters.name: -divide_by / -multiply_by
parameters.description: Integer frequency relationship to the master clock.

parameters.name: -edges
parameters.description: Which master-clock edges form the generated waveform, e.g. {1 3 5} for a divide-by-2.

parameters.name: -edge_shift
parameters.description: Per-edge shift in nanoseconds; used together with -edges to model duty-cycle changes.

parameters.name: -invert
parameters.description: Generated clock is inverted with respect to the master.

parameters.name: -name
parameters.description: Name of the new clock object.

tools.example:
# Divide-by-2 built from a toggling flip-flop
create_generated_clock -name clk_div2 \
  -source [get_pins clk_div_reg/C] -divide_by 2 [get_pins clk_div_reg/Q]

# Clock forwarded off-chip through an ODDR
create_generated_clock -name clk_fwd \
  -source [get_pins oddr_inst/C] -multiply_by 1 [get_ports clk_out]

report_clocks
tools.notes: The -source pin and the constrained object must be on the same clock path. If Vivado already auto-derived a clock at that point, add -add or rename it, otherwise the generated clock silently replaces the derived one.

tools.name: set_input_delay
tools.description: Model how long after the reference clock edge data arrives at an input port, so the timing engine can check the setup and hold requirement of the first capture flop inside the device. Without it, input paths are simply not timed. The numbers come from the driving device's datasheet plus board trace delay, and both a -max (setup) and a -min (hold) value should be supplied.

parameters.name: -clock
parameters.description: Clock object the delay is measured against, from get_clocks. May be a virtual clock.

parameters.name: -max / -min
parameters.description: Latest and earliest data arrival, used for setup and hold analysis respectively.

parameters.name: -clock_fall
parameters.description: Reference the falling edge, for DDR or falling-edge-launched interfaces.

parameters.name: -add_delay
parameters.description: Keep any delay already set on the port instead of replacing it; needed when a port is constrained against two clocks or both edges.

parameters.name: <port_objects>
parameters.description: Ports from get_ports, normally a bus pattern such as {din[*]}.

tools.example:
# Source-synchronous input aligned to a 125 MHz clock
set_input_delay -clock rx_clk -max 3.200 [get_ports {rxd[*]}]
set_input_delay -clock rx_clk -min 1.100 [get_ports {rxd[*]}]

# DDR: constrain both edges
set_input_delay -clock rx_clk -max 1.4 -clock_fall -add_delay [get_ports {rxd[*]}]
set_input_delay -clock rx_clk -min 0.4 -clock_fall -add_delay [get_ports {rxd[*]}]
tools.notes: check_timing -override_defaults no_input_delay lists every input port that still has no delay constraint. Asynchronous inputs such as push buttons should get set_false_path instead of a fabricated delay.

tools.name: set_output_delay
tools.description: Model the setup and hold requirement of the external device that receives data from an output port, measured against a reference clock. It is the mirror image of set_input_delay and is what makes output paths timed. Supply both -max (external setup plus board delay) and -min (negative of the external hold margin) so that clock-to-out is checked in both directions.

parameters.name: -clock
parameters.description: Reference clock object from get_clocks; often a virtual clock representing the board clock.

parameters.name: -max / -min
parameters.description: External setup requirement and external hold requirement (usually negative for -min).

parameters.name: -clock_fall
parameters.description: Reference the falling clock edge for DDR outputs.

parameters.name: -add_delay
parameters.description: Add to existing output delays rather than replacing them.

parameters.name: <port_objects>
parameters.description: Output ports from get_ports.

tools.example:
create_clock -period 8.000 -name virt_dac_clk
set_output_delay -clock virt_dac_clk -max  2.500 [get_ports {dac_data[*]}]
set_output_delay -clock virt_dac_clk -min -0.500 [get_ports {dac_data[*]}]

report_timing -to [get_ports {dac_data[*]}] -delay_type max -max_paths 5
tools.notes: A negative -min value is normal and encodes the external device's hold time. Outputs that drive LEDs or other untimed loads should be excluded with set_false_path rather than given invented numbers.

tools.name: set_clock_groups
tools.description: Tell the timing engine that clocks in different groups are not related, so paths between them are not analysed. Use -asynchronous for clocks from independent sources and -logically_exclusive or -physically_exclusive for clocks that exist on the same net but never run at the same time, such as multiplexed clocks. This is the correct way to handle true clock-domain crossings, and it is bidirectional between every pair of groups.

parameters.name: -asynchronous
parameters.description: Clocks come from unrelated sources with no fixed phase relationship.

parameters.name: -logically_exclusive
parameters.description: Clocks are multiplexed and never active at the same time, but can still couple through crosstalk.

parameters.name: -physically_exclusive
parameters.description: Clocks can never physically be present together, e.g. two create_clock definitions on the same port.

parameters.name: -group
parameters.description: One group of clock objects; repeat the switch once per group. Paths inside a group remain timed.

parameters.name: -name
parameters.description: Optional name so the constraint can be found later with get_clock_groups.

tools.example:
set_clock_groups -name async_clks -asynchronous \
  -group [get_clocks -include_generated_clocks sys_clk] \
  -group [get_clocks -include_generated_clocks usb_clk] \
  -group [get_clocks -include_generated_clocks eth_rx_clk]

report_clock_interaction -delay_type min_max -significant_digits 3 -file clk_interaction.rpt
tools.notes: Always use -include_generated_clocks so MMCM outputs follow their parent into the group. Grouping clocks still requires proper CDC synchronisers in the RTL; the constraint only silences the analysis. report_cdc checks that the synchronisers are actually there.

tools.name: set_false_path
tools.description: Remove a path from timing analysis entirely. Typical uses are reset or configuration signals that are synchronised in the receiving domain, static control registers written once at start-up, and outputs that drive untimed loads. It has the highest priority of all timing exceptions, so it wins over set_max_delay and set_multicycle_path on the same path.

parameters.name: -from
parameters.description: Startpoints: clocks, input ports, or sequential cell/clock pins.

parameters.name: -to
parameters.description: Endpoints: clocks, output ports, or sequential data pins.

parameters.name: -through
parameters.description: Pins, ports or nets the path must pass through; several -through switches are ANDed in order.

parameters.name: -setup / -hold
parameters.description: Restrict the exception to one analysis type only.

parameters.name: -reset_path
parameters.description: Clear previous exceptions on the same path before applying this one.

tools.example:
# Externally asynchronous reset, synchronised internally
set_false_path -from [get_ports rst_n]

# Static configuration register read by another domain
set_false_path -from [get_cells cfg_reg[*]] -to [get_cells {sync/cfg_meta_reg[*]}]

# Untimed status LEDs
set_false_path -to [get_ports {led[*]}]
tools.notes: Prefer set_clock_groups for whole clock-domain crossings; set_false_path is for individual paths. Over-using it hides real problems, and a false path still needs a physical synchroniser in the RTL. Use report_exceptions to list what is actually in effect.

tools.name: set_multicycle_path
tools.description: Relax the number of clock cycles a path is allowed to take, for logic that is known not to need a result every cycle, such as a data path behind a clock enable that is active every fourth cycle. It is the safest way to close timing on slow paths without disabling analysis. Setup and hold are moved together by default, so a setup multicycle almost always needs a matching hold multicycle one cycle smaller.

parameters.name: <path_multiplier>
parameters.description: Number of clock cycles the path may take.

parameters.name: -setup / -hold
parameters.description: Which check to move. A setup multicycle of N normally needs a hold multicycle of N-1.

parameters.name: -start / -end
parameters.description: Whether the multiplier counts launch-clock or capture-clock edges; -end is the default for setup, -start for hold.

parameters.name: -from / -to / -through
parameters.description: Path specification, the same as set_false_path.

tools.example:
# Data path enabled once every 4 cycles, same clock domain
set_multicycle_path 4 -setup -from [get_cells src_reg[*]] -to [get_cells dst_reg[*]]
set_multicycle_path 3 -hold  -from [get_cells src_reg[*]] -to [get_cells dst_reg[*]]

report_timing -from [get_cells src_reg[*]] -to [get_cells dst_reg[*]] -max_paths 3
tools.notes: Forgetting the -hold constraint is the classic mistake: the tool then tries to meet an impossibly tight hold requirement and fills the path with route delay. Between different clock domains the -start/-end choice matters and must match which clock the multiplier is counted on.

tools.name: set_max_delay
tools.description: Put an absolute upper bound in nanoseconds on the delay of a path, replacing the normal clock-based setup requirement. It is most often used on asynchronous crossings that still need a bounded skew, for example a multi-bit bus passing through a handshake synchroniser where the data must be stable when the flag arrives. With -datapath_only the clock skew and uncertainty are excluded, which is the recommended form for CDC.

parameters.name: <delay_ns>
parameters.description: Maximum allowed delay in nanoseconds, usually set to the period of the faster of the two clocks.

parameters.name: -datapath_only
parameters.description: Analyse only the data path, ignoring clock skew and uncertainty; also implicitly removes the hold check. The standard choice for asynchronous data buses.

parameters.name: -from / -to / -through
parameters.description: Path specification.

parameters.name: -reset_path
parameters.description: Remove previously applied exceptions on the same path first.

tools.example:
# Asynchronous data bus captured by a handshake flag
set_max_delay -datapath_only 5.000 \
  -from [get_cells {tx_data_reg[*]}] -to [get_cells {rx_data_reg[*]}]

report_timing -from [get_cells {tx_data_reg[*]}] -to [get_cells {rx_data_reg[*]}] -max_paths 5
tools.notes: Priority is lower than set_false_path but higher than set_multicycle_path. Without -datapath_only a hold check is still applied across the asynchronous boundary, which is meaningless and hard to meet.

tools.name: set_min_delay
tools.description: Set an absolute lower bound in nanoseconds on a path's delay, overriding the normal hold requirement. It is far rarer than set_max_delay and is mostly used for custom interfaces where a minimum propagation time must be guaranteed, or to force the router to add delay on a deliberately padded path.

parameters.name: <delay_ns>
parameters.description: Minimum required delay in nanoseconds.

parameters.name: -from / -to / -through
parameters.description: Path specification, same semantics as set_max_delay.

parameters.name: -reset_path
parameters.description: Clear existing exceptions on the path before applying.

tools.example:
set_min_delay 1.200 -from [get_pins strobe_reg/C] -to [get_ports strobe_out]
report_timing -to [get_ports strobe_out] -delay_type min -max_paths 3
tools.notes: Meeting a min delay costs routing resources because the tool must insert detour routing. Consider adding explicit register stages instead when the required delay is large.

tools.name: set_clock_uncertainty
tools.description: Add extra pessimism to the setup and hold checks of a clock or a clock pair, on top of the jitter Vivado already models. Typical uses are reserving margin for effects the tool does not know about, such as board-level jitter on a clock that is not described with set_input_jitter, or deliberately over-constraining a design during exploration.

parameters.name: <uncertainty_ns>
parameters.description: Additional uncertainty in nanoseconds, added to the computed value.

parameters.name: -setup / -hold
parameters.description: Apply to one check only; without either, both are affected.

parameters.name: -from / -to
parameters.description: Apply only to paths launched by one clock and captured by another (inter-clock uncertainty).

parameters.name: <clock_objects>
parameters.description: Clocks the uncertainty applies to, from get_clocks.

tools.example:
# 100 ps of extra board-level margin on the system clock
set_clock_uncertainty -setup 0.100 [get_clocks sys_clk]

# Extra pessimism only on one crossing
set_clock_uncertainty -from [get_clocks clk_a] -to [get_clocks clk_b] 0.250

report_timing_summary -file timing_with_margin.rpt
tools.notes: Remember to remove exploratory over-constraining before sign-off, or the reported slack will not reflect the real design. Use set_input_jitter for genuine source jitter, since the tool then combines it correctly with the internal clocking model.

tools.name: set_clock_latency
tools.description: Describe delay on a clock outside the boundary of the analysis. Source latency (-source) models the delay from the real clock origin to the port, for example a board-level clock buffer or a long PCB trace; network latency models delay from the port into the design. It matters most for source-synchronous interfaces where the same board clock reaches both devices with different delays.

parameters.name: -source
parameters.description: The latency is outside the chip, between the real clock origin and the constrained port.

parameters.name: -early / -late
parameters.description: Earliest and latest possible arrival, used for the optimistic and pessimistic sides of the check.

parameters.name: -max / -min
parameters.description: Latency value used for setup and hold analysis respectively.

parameters.name: <objects>
parameters.description: Clock objects or the clock's source port.

tools.example:
# 1.2 ns of board trace between the oscillator and the FPGA pin
set_clock_latency -source -max 1.200 [get_clocks sys_clk]
set_clock_latency -source -min 0.900 [get_clocks sys_clk]

report_clocks
tools.notes: Vivado models on-chip clock network delay itself, so network latency is rarely needed; source latency is the useful form. Adding the same latency to both the launching and capturing clock has no effect on the slack of paths between them.

tools.name: set_input_jitter
tools.description: Declare the peak-to-peak jitter of a primary clock arriving from outside the device, in nanoseconds. Vivado folds it into the clock uncertainty for every check involving that clock, and propagates it correctly through MMCM and PLL models to the generated clocks. Use the number from the oscillator or upstream clock generator datasheet.

parameters.name: <clock_object>
parameters.description: The primary clock, from get_clocks. Only clocks created with create_clock accept input jitter.

parameters.name: <jitter_ns>
parameters.description: Peak-to-peak jitter in nanoseconds, e.g. 0.050 for 50 ps.

tools.example:
create_clock -period 10.000 -name sys_clk [get_ports sys_clk_p]
set_input_jitter [get_clocks sys_clk] 0.050
set_system_jitter 0.050

report_clocks
tools.notes: Related to set_system_jitter, which sets a global jitter figure applied to all clocks. Input jitter cannot be applied to generated clocks; constrain the master clock instead and let the tool propagate it.

tools.name: set_case_analysis
tools.description: Force a pin or port to a constant logic value for timing analysis, which prunes away the paths that cannot be active in that configuration. The usual applications are selecting one input of a clock multiplexer, disabling a test or debug mode, and tying off a configuration strap so the analysis reflects the mode the board actually runs in.

parameters.name: <value>
parameters.description: 0, 1, rising or falling. The rising/falling forms restrict which clock edge propagates.

parameters.name: <objects>
parameters.description: Ports or cell pins from get_ports / get_pins.

tools.example:
# Board strap selects the 100 MHz clock branch of a BUFGMUX
set_case_analysis 0 [get_pins clk_mux/S]

# Disable a test mode permanently
set_case_analysis 0 [get_ports test_mode]

report_clocks
report_timing_summary -file timing_functional_mode.rpt
tools.notes: Case analysis removes paths from the report, so a design can look clean simply because too much was pruned. Run report_timing_summary once per configuration if the board really supports several modes.

tools.name: set_disable_timing
tools.description: Disable timing analysis through a specific arc inside a cell, from one pin to another. It is a surgical tool for breaking combinational loops that the timing engine cannot resolve, or for cutting a feedback arc through a LUT used as a latch or shift register. Unlike set_false_path, it removes the arc itself rather than a path, so every path using that arc disappears.

parameters.name: -from
parameters.description: Name of the source pin of the arc inside the cell, e.g. I0.

parameters.name: -to
parameters.description: Name of the destination pin of the arc, e.g. O.

parameters.name: <objects>
parameters.description: Cells or pins whose internal arc should be disabled.

tools.example:
# Break a combinational loop through one LUT input
set_disable_timing -from I1 -to O [get_cells ring_osc/lut_inst]

report_timing_summary -file timing_no_loop.rpt
# Loops also show up in:
check_timing -override_defaults loops
tools.notes: Vivado automatically disables one arc of any combinational loop it finds and reports it as a timing loop; use this command to control which arc is cut rather than accepting the tool's choice. Overuse can silently remove real paths.

tools.name: set_bus_skew
tools.description: Constrain the maximum skew between the individual bits of a bus crossing between clock domains, rather than the absolute delay of each bit. It is the right constraint for a gray-coded pointer or a multi-bit CDC bus, where correctness depends on the bits arriving close together rather than fast. Results are checked with report_bus_skew, not with the normal timing report.

parameters.name: <skew_ns>
parameters.description: Maximum allowed skew between the bits, in nanoseconds; commonly one destination clock period.

parameters.name: -from
parameters.description: Launching registers of the bus.

parameters.name: -to
parameters.description: Capturing registers of the bus.

parameters.name: -through
parameters.description: Optional pins or nets the paths must pass through.

tools.example:
set_max_delay -datapath_only 6.000 \
  -from [get_cells {wr_ptr_gray_reg[*]}] -to [get_cells {wr_ptr_sync_reg[*]}]
set_bus_skew 4.000 \
  -from [get_cells {wr_ptr_gray_reg[*]}] -to [get_cells {wr_ptr_sync_reg[*]}]

report_bus_skew -file bus_skew.rpt
tools.notes: Normally paired with a set_max_delay -datapath_only on the same paths. Bus skew violations do not appear in report_timing_summary's usual tables, so report_bus_skew must be run explicitly during sign-off.

tools.name: set_property PACKAGE_PIN
tools.description: Assign a top-level port to a physical package pin. Together with IOSTANDARD it is the minimum constraint every I/O needs before a bitstream can be generated, and Vivado issues a DRC error for any unlocated port. The pin name comes from the package file or the board definition; the I/O Planning layout in the GUI writes exactly this command into the XDC.

parameters.name: PACKAGE_PIN
parameters.description: Package pin designator such as AH11 or E3, valid for the selected part and package.

parameters.name: [get_ports ...]
parameters.description: The top-level port object. Bus bits are addressed individually, e.g. [get_ports {led[0]}].

tools.notes: For a differential pair only the P side needs locating; the N side is implied by the package. Use set_property -dict to set PACKAGE_PIN and IOSTANDARD in one call, and report_io to verify all assignments after implementation.

tools.name: set_property IOSTANDARD
tools.description: Set the electrical I/O standard of a port, which determines the drive strength, termination, reference voltage and the VCCO the bank must run at. Every located port needs one, and all ports in the same I/O bank must use standards compatible with a single VCCO. Related properties DRIVE, SLEW, PULLUP/PULLDOWN, DIFF_TERM and IBUF_LOW_PWR fine-tune the same buffer.
tools.usage:
set_property IOSTANDARD <standard> [get_ports <port_name>]
set_property -dict {PACKAGE_PIN <pin> IOSTANDARD <standard> DRIVE <mA> SLEW <SLOW|FAST>} [get_ports <port>]

parameters.name: IOSTANDARD
parameters.description: e.g. LVCMOS33, LVCMOS18, LVDS, DIFF_SSTL12, SSTL15, HSTL_I, POD12. The set available depends on the bank type (HR/HP/HD).

parameters.name: DRIVE
parameters.description: Output drive current in mA for single-ended CMOS standards, typically 4, 8, 12 or 16.

parameters.name: SLEW
parameters.description: SLOW or FAST output edge rate; SLOW reduces SSN, FAST reduces clock-to-out.

parameters.name: DIFF_TERM
parameters.description: TRUE enables the internal 100 ohm differential termination on LVDS inputs.

parameters.name: PULLUP / PULLDOWN / PULLTYPE
parameters.description: Enable the weak internal pull resistor on an input or bidirectional port.

tools.example:
set_property -dict {PACKAGE_PIN H17 IOSTANDARD LVCMOS33 DRIVE 12 SLEW SLOW} [get_ports {led[0]}]
set_property -dict {PACKAGE_PIN AH11 IOSTANDARD DIFF_SSTL12} [get_ports sys_clk_p]
set_property DIFF_TERM TRUE [get_ports rx_p]

report_io -file io.rpt
tools.notes: High-performance (HP) banks cannot drive 3.3 V standards; choosing LVCMOS33 on an HP bank is a common DRC failure. report_io shows the resolved standard, bank and VCCO for every port.

tools.name: set_property LOC
tools.description: Lock a cell to a specific site on the device, such as a slice, block RAM, DSP, MMCM or I/O buffer. Use it sparingly: the placer is usually better than a human, and hard placement constraints often hurt the rest of the design. The legitimate cases are clocking resources that must sit in a particular clock region, IOB registers, and reproducing a known-good placement captured from an earlier run.

parameters.name: LOC
parameters.description: Site name such as SLICE_X10Y50, RAMB36_X2Y10, MMCME4_ADV_X0Y1 or IOB_X0Y12.

parameters.name: BEL
parameters.description: The specific element within the site, e.g. AFF or A6LUT. Normally set together with LOC.

parameters.name: [get_cells ...]
parameters.description: Leaf cell object; use -hierarchical with a filter to find cells deep in the hierarchy.

tools.example:
set_property LOC MMCME4_ADV_X0Y1 [get_cells clk_gen/mmcm_inst]
set_property LOC RAMB36_X3Y20   [get_cells buffer/ram_reg_0]
set_property BEL AFF            [get_cells pipe/out_reg]
set_property LOC SLICE_X12Y88   [get_cells pipe/out_reg]

place_design
report_utilization -file util.rpt
tools.notes: Site names differ between devices, so LOC constraints are not portable across parts. To capture an existing placement, open the implemented design and use write_xdc with the appropriate options rather than typing sites by hand.

tools.name: create_pblock
tools.description: Create a physical block: a named rectangular region of the device that a set of cells is constrained into. Pblocks are used to keep a critical module compact, to isolate a partially reconfigurable region, to separate unrelated clock domains physically, or to reserve area. The family of commands is create_pblock to define it, add_cells_to_pblock to populate it and resize_pblock to give it a shape.

parameters.name: -add
parameters.description: Site ranges the pblock covers, given as START:END pairs per resource type.

parameters.name: -remove
parameters.description: Remove site ranges from an existing pblock.

parameters.name: -clear_locs
parameters.description: Drop any existing LOC constraints on the cells being added.

parameters.name: CONTAIN_ROUTING
parameters.description: Pblock property; TRUE forces routing as well as logic to stay inside the region (required for Dynamic Function eXchange).

parameters.name: EXCLUDE_PLACEMENT
parameters.description: Pblock property; TRUE stops cells that are not members from being placed inside the region.

tools.example:
create_pblock pblock_dsp
add_cells_to_pblock [get_pblocks pblock_dsp] [get_cells -quiet [list dsp_chain]]
resize_pblock [get_pblocks pblock_dsp] -add {SLICE_X40Y120:SLICE_X70Y179 DSP48E2_X6Y48:DSP48E2_X9Y71}
set_property CONTAIN_ROUTING true [get_pblocks pblock_dsp]

place_design
report_utilization -pblocks [get_pblocks pblock_dsp] -file pblock_util.rpt
tools.notes: A pblock that is too tight causes placement congestion and worse timing than no pblock at all; check with report_utilization -pblocks that occupancy stays well under 100%. The GUI Floorplanning layout draws pblocks and writes these same commands.

tools.name: set_property CLOCK_DEDICATED_ROUTE
tools.description: Relax the rule that a clock must travel on dedicated clock routing from its source to its buffer. Vivado raises a Placer error when a clock-capable pin drives a global buffer in a different clock region or half of the device, and this property downgrades that to a warning so the design can be routed on general fabric. It is a deliberate escape hatch, not a fix, and should only be used when the resulting jitter and skew are acceptable.

parameters.name: FALSE
parameters.description: Allow the clock to use general routing resources; the most common override.

parameters.name: BACKBONE
parameters.description: Allow routing on the clock backbone across regions while still using dedicated resources.

parameters.name: ANY_CMT_COLUMN / SAME_CMT_COLUMN
parameters.description: Restrict how far the clock may travel between clock management tile columns.

parameters.name: <net>
parameters.description: The clock net, usually the output of the IBUF feeding the BUFG, found with get_nets -of_objects.

tools.example:
# Clock enters on a pin in a different region from its BUFG
set_property CLOCK_DEDICATED_ROUTE FALSE [get_nets clk_in_IBUF]

place_design
report_clock_networks -file clock_networks.rpt
report_methodology -file methodology.rpt
tools.notes: Always check report_clock_networks and the resulting skew afterwards. The correct long-term fix is to move the clock to a clock-capable pin in the right region, or to re-plan the clock regions.

tools.name: set_property ASYNC_REG
tools.description: Mark the flip-flops of a synchroniser chain so the tools treat them specially: they are kept, not optimised away or retimed, and the placer puts them in the same slice to minimise the routing delay between stages and maximise mean time between failures. Apply it to every stage of every two- or three-flop synchroniser in the design. report_cdc checks that synchronisers it finds carry this attribute.
tools.usage:
set_property ASYNC_REG TRUE [get_cells <synchroniser_registers>]
(* ASYNC_REG = "TRUE" *) reg [1:0] sync_ff;   // RTL attribute form

parameters.name: ASYNC_REG
parameters.description: TRUE marks the register as part of an asynchronous clock-domain crossing.

parameters.name: [get_cells ...]
parameters.description: The synchroniser flip-flops; -hierarchical with a NAME filter is the usual way to catch them all.

tools.example:
set_property ASYNC_REG TRUE [get_cells -hierarchical -filter {NAME =~ *sync_ff_reg[*]}]

# Equivalent attribute in SystemVerilog source
# (* ASYNC_REG = "TRUE" *) logic [1:0] meta_q;

report_cdc -file cdc.rpt
tools.notes: ASYNC_REG on its own does not constrain timing; pair it with set_clock_groups or set_max_delay -datapath_only so the crossing is not analysed as a synchronous path. Putting it in the RTL is usually more maintainable than a wildcard XDC match.

tools.name: set_property MARK_DEBUG
tools.description: Flag a net so it survives synthesis optimisation and appears in the debug net list, ready to be connected to an ILA core. It is the netlist-insertion path to debug: mark the nets, run the Set Up Debug wizard or the create_debug_core commands, and the probes appear in the Hardware Manager. Marked nets are not optimised away or renamed, which slightly constrains synthesis.
tools.usage:
set_property MARK_DEBUG TRUE [get_nets <net_names>]
(* MARK_DEBUG = "TRUE" *) wire [7:0] state;   // RTL attribute form

parameters.name: MARK_DEBUG
parameters.description: TRUE preserves the net and adds it to the debug candidates list.

parameters.name: [get_nets ...]
parameters.description: Nets to preserve; -hierarchical with a filter finds them inside submodules.

tools.example:
set_property MARK_DEBUG TRUE [get_nets {fsm/state_reg[*]}]
set_property MARK_DEBUG TRUE [get_nets -hierarchical -filter {NAME =~ *axi_awvalid}]

# Then attach the marked nets to an ILA
create_debug_core u_ila_0 ila
set_property C_DATA_DEPTH 4096 [get_debug_cores u_ila_0]
connect_debug_port u_ila_0/clk [get_nets clk_100]
write_debug_probes -force debug_nets.ltx
tools.notes: Marked nets block optimisations, so remove the attribute for production builds. DONT_TOUCH has a similar preservation effect but does not add the net to the debug list.

tools.name: set_property DONT_TOUCH
tools.description: Stop synthesis and implementation from optimising away, merging or renaming a cell or net. Use it to preserve a module boundary for partial reconfiguration, keep a deliberately redundant register such as a reset synchroniser, or hold on to a signal for probing. The related KEEP_HIERARCHY property preserves a hierarchy boundary through synthesis instead of a single object.
tools.usage:
set_property DONT_TOUCH TRUE [get_cells <cell>]
set_property KEEP_HIERARCHY TRUE [get_cells <hierarchical_cell>]

parameters.name: DONT_TOUCH
parameters.description: TRUE preserves the object through synthesis, opt_design and physical optimisation.

parameters.name: KEEP_HIERARCHY
parameters.description: TRUE stops synthesis flattening across that module boundary, which keeps names stable for constraints and reports.

parameters.name: <objects>
parameters.description: Cells or nets; applies to the object and, for a hierarchical cell, to everything inside it.

tools.example:
set_property DONT_TOUCH TRUE [get_cells reset_sync_inst]
set_property KEEP_HIERARCHY TRUE [get_cells dsp_pipeline_inst]

synth_design -top top -part xcku040-ffva1156-2-e
report_utilization -hierarchical -file util_hier.rpt
tools.notes: DONT_TOUCH also blocks retiming and register merging, so it can cost timing. Prefer the RTL attribute form (* dont_touch = "true" *) so the intent lives with the code, and remove it when it is no longer needed.

tools.name: set_property BITSTREAM.*
tools.description: Configure how the bitstream is generated and how the device boots, by setting BITSTREAM.* properties on the current design before write_bitstream. These control the configuration rate and bus width, whether unused pins are pulled up, compression, encryption, and the behaviour of the CRC and start-up sequence. They are usually placed in the XDC alongside CFGBVS and CONFIG_VOLTAGE.

parameters.name: BITSTREAM.GENERAL.COMPRESS
parameters.description: TRUE enables bitstream compression, reducing file size and configuration time.

parameters.name: BITSTREAM.CONFIG.CONFIGRATE
parameters.description: Configuration clock rate in MHz for master modes, e.g. 33, 50, 66.

parameters.name: BITSTREAM.CONFIG.SPI_BUSWIDTH
parameters.description: 1, 2, 4 or 8 for x1/x2/x4/x8 SPI flash configuration.

parameters.name: BITSTREAM.CONFIG.UNUSEDPIN
parameters.description: PULLUP, PULLDOWN or PULLNONE for pins not used by the design.

parameters.name: BITSTREAM.GENERAL.CRC
parameters.description: ENABLE or DISABLE the configuration CRC check.

parameters.name: BITSTREAM.ENCRYPTION.ENCRYPT
parameters.description: YES enables AES bitstream encryption; used with ENCRYPTKEYSELECT and a key file.

tools.example:
set_property CFGBVS VCCO [current_design]
set_property CONFIG_VOLTAGE 3.3 [current_design]
set_property BITSTREAM.GENERAL.COMPRESS TRUE [current_design]
set_property BITSTREAM.CONFIG.CONFIGRATE 50 [current_design]
set_property BITSTREAM.CONFIG.SPI_BUSWIDTH 4 [current_design]
set_property BITSTREAM.CONFIG.UNUSEDPIN PULLUP [current_design]

write_bitstream -force ./top.bit
write_cfgmem -format mcs -interface SPIx4 -size 64 -loadbit "up 0x0 ./top.bit" -force ./top.mcs
tools.notes: CFGBVS and CONFIG_VOLTAGE must match the board's bank 0 voltage or write_bitstream issues a DRC error. Options are device-family specific; `list_property [current_design]` shows every BITSTREAM.* property the selected part supports.

tools.name: report_timing
tools.description: Report detailed timing for individual paths, showing every cell and net delay from startpoint to endpoint with the arrival and required times. Use it when report_timing_summary has told you which endpoint is failing and you need to see where the delay actually goes. The -from/-through/-to filters and -max_paths let you aim it at exactly the paths you care about.

parameters.name: -delay_type
parameters.description: max for setup, min for hold, min_max for both.

parameters.name: -max_paths
parameters.description: Total number of paths to report; -nworst limits how many are reported per endpoint.

parameters.name: -path_type
parameters.description: How much detail to print; full_clock also shows the clock path, which is essential for skew debugging.

parameters.name: -input_pins
parameters.description: Show delay at every input pin along the path, not just the cell outputs.

parameters.name: -file / -append
parameters.description: Write to a text file instead of the console.

parameters.name: -name
parameters.description: Open the result as an interactive GUI window with cross-probing to the schematic and device view.

tools.example:
report_timing -from [get_cells fifo/wr_ptr_reg[*]] -to [get_cells fifo/rd_sync_reg[*]] \
  -delay_type max -max_paths 10 -nworst 2 -path_type full_clock -input_pins \
  -file ./reports/fifo_paths.rpt

# 20 worst setup paths in the whole design, as a GUI window
report_timing -delay_type max -max_paths 20 -sort_by slack -name worst_setup
tools.notes: report_timing only analyses the design currently in memory, so open a routed checkpoint or run route_design first if you want real routing delays. get_timing_paths returns the same information as Tcl objects for scripting.

tools.name: report_timing_summary
tools.description: The sign-off timing report. It runs the equivalent of check_timing, lists worst negative slack, total negative slack and failing endpoints for setup, hold and pulse-width checks per clock, and shows the worst paths in each clock group. Run it after route_design on every build and store the output; if WNS and WHS are both non-negative and there are no unconstrained endpoints, timing is closed.

parameters.name: -delay_type
parameters.description: min_max reports setup and hold together (the default for sign-off).

parameters.name: -max_paths
parameters.description: Number of paths listed per path group.

parameters.name: -report_unconstrained
parameters.description: Include endpoints with no timing constraint, which is how missing constraints are found.

parameters.name: -check_timing_verbose
parameters.description: Embed a full check_timing section in the report.

parameters.name: -warn_on_violation
parameters.description: Emit a critical warning when a violation is found, so a scripted build can react to it.

parameters.name: -file / -name
parameters.description: Write to a file, or open as an interactive GUI window.

tools.example:
route_design
report_timing_summary -delay_type min_max -max_paths 10 -report_unconstrained \
  -check_timing_verbose -warn_on_violation -file ./reports/timing_summary.rpt

# Gate a scripted build on the result
set wns [get_property SLACK [get_timing_paths -delay_type max]]
if {$wns < 0} { error "Timing not met: WNS = $wns ns" }
tools.notes: Intra-clock, inter-clock and other path-group tables are separate; a design can show WNS met overall while an inter-clock group is badly violated, so read all sections. Always check the unconstrained-endpoint count, which is the single most common cause of a false pass.

tools.name: report_clocks
tools.description: List every clock the timing engine knows about, including user-defined primary clocks, auto-derived MMCM and PLL outputs, and generated clocks, with their period, waveform, source and whether they are propagated. It is the first thing to run after loading constraints, because a missing or duplicated clock explains most strange timing results.

parameters.name: <clock_objects>
parameters.description: Restrict the report to specific clocks from get_clocks; without it, all clocks are listed.

parameters.name: -file / -append
parameters.description: Write or append to a text file.

parameters.name: -return_string
parameters.description: Return the report as a Tcl string for scripted parsing.

tools.example:
read_xdc ./constrs/top.xdc
synth_design -top top -part xcku040-ffva1156-2-e
report_clocks -file ./reports/clocks.rpt

# List clock names and periods programmatically
foreach c [get_clocks] {
  puts [format "%-20s %8.3f ns" $c [get_property PERIOD $c]]
}
tools.notes: Look for clocks with the same name defined twice, clocks whose period does not match the hardware, and auto-derived clocks whose names change between releases. report_clock_networks shows the physical distribution of the same clocks.

tools.name: report_clock_interaction
tools.description: Produce a matrix of every pair of clocks that has paths between them, showing whether the crossing is constrained, partially constrained through exceptions, asynchronous or unsafe. It is the main tool for verifying that set_clock_groups and set_false_path cover all the real clock-domain crossings, and for finding crossings nobody knew existed.

parameters.name: -delay_type
parameters.description: Which analysis to base the matrix on; min_max covers setup and hold.

parameters.name: -significant_digits
parameters.description: Number of decimal places in the reported slack values.

parameters.name: -file
parameters.description: Write the matrix to a text file.

parameters.name: -name
parameters.description: Open as a GUI window where each cell can be cross-probed to the offending paths.

tools.example:
report_clock_interaction -delay_type min_max -significant_digits 3 \
  -file ./reports/clock_interaction.rpt -name clk_matrix

# Then close the genuinely asynchronous ones
set_clock_groups -asynchronous \
  -group [get_clocks -include_generated_clocks sys_clk] \
  -group [get_clocks -include_generated_clocks eth_rx_clk]
tools.notes: Pay attention to pairs marked as having no common period or as partially false path: those are the ones that will fail intermittently in hardware. Pair this report with report_cdc, which checks the structure of the synchronisers rather than the constraints.

tools.name: report_cdc
tools.description: Structurally analyse every clock-domain crossing in the design and classify it by safety: properly synchronised multi-flop chains, asynchronous resets, combinational logic feeding a synchroniser, missing ASYNC_REG attributes, fan-out from a single synchroniser, and unsafe direct crossings. Unlike the timing reports it looks at the circuit, so it catches CDC bugs that constraints have hidden.

parameters.name: -details
parameters.description: Print every individual crossing rather than a summary count per severity.

parameters.name: -severity
parameters.description: Filter to Critical, Warning or Info level findings.

parameters.name: -file / -name
parameters.description: Write to a file or open as a cross-probing GUI window.

parameters.name: -from / -to
parameters.description: Restrict the analysis to crossings between specific clocks.

tools.example:
synth_design -top top -part xcku040-ffva1156-2-e
report_cdc -details -file ./reports/cdc.rpt

# Fix the usual finding: missing ASYNC_REG on synchroniser chains
set_property ASYNC_REG TRUE [get_cells -hierarchical -filter {NAME =~ *sync_ff_reg[*]}]
report_cdc -severity Critical
tools.notes: Run it on the synthesized design, before placement, so findings can still be fixed in RTL. A Critical finding almost always means a genuine metastability hazard, not a constraint problem; report_clock_interaction covers the constraint side.

tools.name: report_methodology
tools.description: Run the Vivado methodology rule checks, which flag constraint and design practices that are technically legal but known to cause trouble: missing input/output delays, clocks without jitter, latches, multi-driven nets, unsafe CDC, badly constrained MMCMs, and inefficient synchronous resets. It is part of the expected sign-off flow alongside report_drc and report_timing_summary.

parameters.name: -checks
parameters.description: Run only named checks, e.g. TIMING-6 or SYNTH-9.

parameters.name: -ruledecks
parameters.description: Run a predefined bundle of checks, such as the default methodology rule deck.

parameters.name: -file / -name
parameters.description: Write to a text file or open a cross-probing GUI window.

parameters.name: -waived
parameters.description: Report only violations that have been waived with create_waiver.

tools.example:
opt_design
report_methodology -file ./reports/methodology.rpt -name methodology

# Waive a reviewed and accepted finding so future runs stay clean
create_waiver -type METHODOLOGY -id TIMING-18 \
  -objects [get_cells sync/meta_reg] -description "Reviewed CDC, 3FF sync in place"
tools.notes: Run it after synthesis and again after opt_design; some checks need a placed design. Waive findings with create_waiver rather than ignoring them, so the report stays meaningful and the waiver carries a written justification.

tools.name: report_drc
tools.description: Run design rule checks against the current design, covering I/O bank and voltage legality, clocking resource placement, unconnected or multi-driven nets, block configuration problems and bitstream-generation prerequisites. It runs automatically before write_bitstream, and errors there will stop the build, so running it early after opt_design saves a lot of time.

parameters.name: -checks
parameters.description: Run specific DRC rules only, e.g. NSTD-1 or UCIO-1.

parameters.name: -ruledecks
parameters.description: Named rule bundle: default, opt_checks, placer_checks, router_checks, bitstream_checks, timing_checks.

parameters.name: -file / -name
parameters.description: Write the report to a file, or open as a GUI window with cross-probing.

parameters.name: -upgrade_cw
parameters.description: Promote critical warnings to errors so a scripted build fails on them.

tools.example:
opt_design
report_drc -ruledecks {default} -file ./reports/drc_opt.rpt

route_design
report_drc -ruledecks {bitstream_checks} -file ./reports/drc_bitstream.rpt
write_bitstream -force ./top.bit
tools.notes: UCIO-1 (unspecified I/O standard) and NSTD-1 (unspecified I/O location) are the two rules that most often block bitstream generation; both come from missing PACKAGE_PIN or IOSTANDARD constraints. Genuine false positives can be silenced with create_waiver -type DRC.

tools.name: report_utilization
tools.description: Report resource usage for the current design: LUTs, registers, CARRY chains, F7/F8 muxes, block RAM, URAM, DSP slices, I/O, clocking resources and, on SoC devices, the processor subsystem. Run it after synthesis for an early estimate and after implementation for the real number, and use -hierarchical to find which module is consuming the resources.

parameters.name: -hierarchical
parameters.description: Break the usage down per module instead of reporting only device totals.

parameters.name: -hierarchical_depth
parameters.description: How many levels of hierarchy to show.

parameters.name: -pblocks
parameters.description: Report utilisation inside specific pblocks, to check a floorplan is not over-full.

parameters.name: -slr
parameters.description: Report per super logic region on stacked-silicon devices.

parameters.name: -file / -append
parameters.description: Write or append to a text file.

tools.example:
synth_design -top top -part xcvu9p-flga2104-2L-e
report_utilization -hierarchical -hierarchical_depth 3 -file ./reports/util_synth.rpt

place_design
report_utilization -slr -file ./reports/util_slr.rpt
report_utilization -pblocks [get_pblocks pblock_dsp] -file ./reports/util_pblock.rpt
tools.notes: Synthesis numbers are optimistic because opt_design and physical optimisation still change the netlist. If block RAM or DSP usage is unexpectedly high, check the synth_design -max_bram / -max_dsp limits and the inference of your RTL.

tools.name: report_power
tools.description: Estimate static and dynamic power for the current design, broken down by clocks, logic, signals, block RAM, DSP, I/O and any hard blocks, along with junction temperature and thermal margin. Accuracy depends entirely on switching activity, so feed it a SAIF file from simulation with read_saif, or set activity rates explicitly with set_switching_activity, before trusting the numbers.

parameters.name: -advisory
parameters.description: Include advice on how to improve the confidence level and reduce power.

parameters.name: -hier
parameters.description: Report power per hierarchy level.

parameters.name: -xpe
parameters.description: Write an .xpe file that can be opened in the Xilinx Power Estimator spreadsheet.

parameters.name: -file / -name
parameters.description: Write to a text file or open a GUI window.

tools.example:
open_checkpoint ./post_route.dcp
read_saif -strip_path tb/dut ./sim/postimpl.saif
set_switching_activity -default_toggle_rate 25.0 -default_static_probability 0.5
report_power -advisory -file ./reports/power.rpt -xpe ./reports/power.xpe

# Power optimisation in the flow
opt_design
power_opt_design
place_design
tools.notes: The report prints a confidence level (Low/Medium/High); Low almost always means no switching activity was supplied. power_opt_design applies clock gating to reduce dynamic power and can be run after opt_design or after place_design.

tools.name: report_design_analysis
tools.description: Deep-dive analysis of what is limiting quality of results: the composition of the critical paths (logic levels, net delay share, fan-out, SLR crossings), congestion levels per device region, and the complexity of the netlist. It is the report to open when timing fails but no single path looks obviously wrong, because it shows whether the problem is logic depth, routing congestion or placement spread.

parameters.name: -timing
parameters.description: Analyse the critical paths, showing delay split between logic and routing.

parameters.name: -congestion
parameters.description: Report placer and router congestion levels per region, which explains long runtimes and unroutable designs.

parameters.name: -complexity
parameters.description: Report Rent exponent and average fan-out, indicating how hard the netlist is to place.

parameters.name: -logic_level_distribution
parameters.description: Histogram of logic levels per path group; a long tail points at paths needing pipelining.

parameters.name: -of_timing_paths
parameters.description: Analyse a specific set of paths returned by get_timing_paths.

tools.example:
open_checkpoint ./post_route.dcp
report_design_analysis -timing -setup -logic_level_distribution \
  -of_timing_paths [get_timing_paths -max_paths 50 -delay_type max] \
  -file ./reports/design_analysis.rpt

report_design_analysis -congestion -complexity -file ./reports/congestion.rpt
tools.notes: A high net-delay share with few logic levels usually means congestion or placement spread rather than logic depth. Congestion levels of 5 or above in a region typically require floorplanning or RTL restructuring rather than a different implementation directive.

tools.name: report_route_status
tools.description: Summarise the routing state of every net in the design: fully routed, partially routed, unrouted, or having routing conflicts. It is the quickest way to confirm that route_design actually finished, and to find the specific nets that failed when it did not. A design with any unrouted or conflicted nets cannot produce a valid bitstream.

parameters.name: -of_objects
parameters.description: Report only on specific nets from get_nets.

parameters.name: -list_all_nets
parameters.description: List every net and its individual status rather than only the summary counts.

parameters.name: -show_all
parameters.description: Include nets in every status category, including fully routed ones.

parameters.name: -file / -name
parameters.description: Write to a text file or open as a GUI window.

tools.example:
route_design
report_route_status -file ./reports/route_status.rpt

# Find and inspect any nets that failed to route
set bad [get_nets -filter {ROUTE_STATUS != ROUTED && ROUTE_STATUS != INTRASITE}]
if {[llength $bad]} {
  report_route_status -of_objects $bad -list_all_nets
}
tools.notes: Unrouted nets almost always come from congestion or an over-tight pblock. Re-running route_design with a different -directive such as Explore or AlternateCLBRouting, or loosening the floorplan, is the usual remedy.

tools.name: check_timing
tools.description: Audit the constraint set itself rather than the timing results, listing unconstrained internal endpoints, ports with no input or output delay, clocks with no period, combinational loops, partially constrained I/O and multiple clocks reaching the same register. Run it immediately after reading the XDC, because almost every case of 'timing met but the board does not work' starts with a finding here.

parameters.name: -override_defaults
parameters.description: Run only the named checks, e.g. no_clock, no_input_delay, no_output_delay, unconstrained_internal_endpoints, loops, multiple_clock.

parameters.name: -include / -exclude
parameters.description: Add to or remove from the default check list.

parameters.name: -verbose
parameters.description: List every affected object instead of a count.

parameters.name: -file / -name
parameters.description: Write to a text file or open as a GUI window.

tools.example:
read_xdc ./constrs/top.xdc
synth_design -top top -part xcku040-ffva1156-2-e
check_timing -verbose -file ./reports/check_timing.rpt

# Just the two checks that matter most for board bring-up
check_timing -override_defaults {no_input_delay no_output_delay} -verbose
tools.notes: report_timing_summary -check_timing_verbose embeds the same information in the sign-off report. A non-zero unconstrained_internal_endpoints count means part of the design is simply not being timed.

tools.name: get_cells
tools.description: Query the netlist for cell objects, which are then passed to constraints, properties and reports. The -hierarchical switch searches the whole design rather than the current level, -filter applies a property expression, and -of_objects walks from pins or nets to the cells attached to them. Together with get_ports, get_nets and get_pins it is the backbone of every non-trivial XDC file.

parameters.name: -hierarchical
parameters.description: Search every level of hierarchy. The pattern then matches the leaf name, so use -filter {NAME =~ ...} to match full paths.

parameters.name: -filter
parameters.description: Property expression, e.g. {REF_NAME == FDRE && IS_PRIMITIVE} or {NAME =~ *sync_reg*}.

parameters.name: -of_objects
parameters.description: Return the cells connected to the given pins, nets or sites.

parameters.name: -regexp / -nocase
parameters.description: Interpret patterns as regular expressions and ignore case.

parameters.name: -quiet
parameters.description: Return an empty list instead of an error when nothing matches; essential in scripts that run before synthesis.

tools.example:
# Every flip-flop in a synchroniser, anywhere in the hierarchy
set_property ASYNC_REG TRUE [get_cells -hierarchical -filter {NAME =~ *sync_ff_reg[*]}]

# All block RAMs, for a utilisation sanity check
puts "BRAMs: [llength [get_cells -hierarchical -filter {PRIMITIVE_TYPE =~ BMEM.*.*}]]"

# Filter an existing collection further
set ffs [get_cells -hier -filter {IS_SEQUENTIAL}]
puts [llength [filter $ffs {NAME =~ *dsp_pipeline*}]]
tools.notes: In an XDC read before synthesis only ports exist, so get_cells returns nothing; scope cell constraints to the synthesized design or mark the XDC USED_IN_SYNTHESIS false. The filter command applies the same expression syntax to an already-retrieved collection.

tools.name: get_ports
tools.description: Return top-level port objects, the targets of virtually every physical and I/O timing constraint. Patterns support wildcards for buses, and -filter selects on properties such as DIRECTION, IOSTANDARD or PACKAGE_PIN. Because ports exist in the elaborated design, get_ports works in XDC files read before synthesis, unlike get_cells and get_nets.

parameters.name: <patterns>
parameters.description: Port name patterns; brace bus patterns such as {led[*]} so Tcl does not treat the brackets as command substitution.

parameters.name: -filter
parameters.description: Property expression, e.g. {DIRECTION == IN} or {IOSTANDARD == LVCMOS33}.

parameters.name: -of_objects
parameters.description: Return ports connected to given nets or clocks.

parameters.name: -quiet
parameters.description: Suppress the error when no port matches.

tools.notes: Always brace bus patterns: get_ports led[*] without braces is a Tcl syntax error, while get_ports {led[*]} works. all_inputs and all_outputs are convenient shorthands for the common direction filters.

tools.name: get_timing_paths
tools.description: Return timing paths as first-class Tcl objects rather than printed text, so a script can read SLACK, STARTPOINT_PIN, ENDPOINT_PIN, LOGIC_LEVELS and other properties and act on them. This is how a build script gates on WNS, how a report is turned into CSV, and how report_design_analysis is aimed at a specific set of paths.

parameters.name: -delay_type
parameters.description: max for setup paths, min for hold paths.

parameters.name: -max_paths / -nworst
parameters.description: How many paths to return in total and per endpoint.

parameters.name: -slack_lesser_than
parameters.description: Return only paths whose slack is below a threshold, which is the efficient way to find violators.

parameters.name: -from / -to / -through
parameters.description: Path filters, identical to report_timing.

parameters.name: -sort_by
parameters.description: slack or group ordering of the returned collection.

tools.example:
route_design
set wns [get_property SLACK [lindex [get_timing_paths -delay_type max -max_paths 1] 0]]
puts "WNS = $wns ns"

# Dump every violating path to CSV
set fh [open ./reports/violations.csv w]
puts $fh "slack,levels,startpoint,endpoint"
foreach p [get_timing_paths -delay_type max -slack_lesser_than 0 -max_paths 1000] {
  puts $fh "[get_property SLACK $p],[get_property LOGIC_LEVELS $p],\
[get_property STARTPOINT_PIN $p],[get_property ENDPOINT_PIN $p]"
}
close $fh
tools.notes: report_property on a path object lists every readable property. Paths are only meaningful for the design currently in memory, so open the routed checkpoint first if you want post-route slack.

tools.name: all_registers
tools.description: Return the sequential cells or their pins, optionally restricted to one clock or to a particular kind of pin. It is the natural startpoint or endpoint collection for broad timing exceptions and for writing constraints that apply to a whole clock domain. The companion commands all_clocks, all_inputs, all_outputs, all_fanin and all_fanout cover the other common collections.

parameters.name: -clock
parameters.description: Only registers clocked by the given clock object.

parameters.name: -cells
parameters.description: Return cell objects instead of the default pin objects.

parameters.name: -data_pins / -clock_pins / -output_pins
parameters.description: Return a specific pin of each register, e.g. the D, C or Q pin.

parameters.name: -edge_triggered / -level_sensitive
parameters.description: Restrict to flip-flops or to latches respectively; -level_sensitive is a quick way to find unintended latches.

tools.example:
# Cut all paths from a slow configuration domain into the fast one
set_false_path -from [all_registers -clock cfg_clk] -to [all_registers -clock core_clk]

# Count flip-flops per clock
foreach c [all_clocks] {
  puts "$c : [llength [all_registers -clock $c -cells]]"
}

# Trace what drives a failing endpoint
report_timing -to [get_pins fifo/dout_reg[0]/D] -max_paths 1
puts [get_cells -of_objects [all_fanin -flat -startpoints_only [get_pins fifo/dout_reg[0]/D]]]
tools.notes: Prefer set_clock_groups over a blanket set_false_path between two all_registers collections: the clock-group form also covers generated clocks and future registers automatically. all_fanin/all_fanout accept -flat and -only_cells to control how far they walk.
